sections.title: Paper 2B: gas exchange follows concentration gradients
paragraphs: Carbon dioxide and oxygen move through a leaf by diffusion. Random molecular movement produces net movement from higher to lower concentration, while molecules still move in both directions. A gas concentration difference is not an active pumping mechanism.

Gas moves between the outside air, stomatal pores and internal leaf air spaces. It then dissolves at moist cell surfaces before crossing cell membranes. Photosynthesis and respiration change local gas concentrations and therefore influence the gradients.

The direction for one gas need not match the other. In strong light, a photosynthesising leaf may have net carbon-dioxide entry and net oxygen exit. In darkness, respiration can give the opposite net directions.

example.question: Does carbon dioxide always move out of a living leaf?
steps: No. Its net direction depends on relative concentrations.
Photosynthetic uptake in suitable light can support net inward diffusion.
Respiration in darkness can support net outward diffusion.
example.explanation: Connect the gas-specific concentration difference to net movement.

practice.question: Is diffusion the same as air being pumped through a leaf?
practice.answer: No. It is net molecular movement down a concentration gradient.
practice.explanation: Connect the gas-specific concentration difference to net movement.

commonMistakes: Use a net direction rather than claiming all molecules travel only one way.

sections.title: Paper 2B: interpret photosynthesis and respiration together
paragraphs: Respiration continues in living leaf cells during both day and night. Photosynthesis needs light and can remove carbon dioxide while releasing oxygen. The observed net exchange combines the contributions of both processes.

In darkness, photosynthesis is absent and respiratory carbon-dioxide production can exceed uptake, giving net carbon-dioxide release and oxygen uptake. In sufficiently bright light, photosynthesis can exceed respiration, giving net carbon-dioxide uptake and oxygen release.

At the compensation condition, the photosynthetic carbon-dioxide uptake rate balances respiratory release, so net exchange is approximately zero. Both processes can still be occurring; zero net exchange is not proof that metabolism stopped.

For a clearly hypothetical arithmetic model, in common rate units, photosynthesis removes 8 units of carbon dioxide while respiration releases 3, so net uptake is 5. If both rates are 3, net exchange is 0. These numbers are a model, not measured biological rates.

example.question: Photosynthesis removes 8 units of CO₂ per interval and respiration releases 3 in the same units. Find the net exchange.
steps: Respiration continues despite the inward net carbon-dioxide movement.
At equal rates, the two contributions cancel in the net measurement.
example.explanation: Subtract opposing rates expressed on the same basis and retain both underlying processes.

practice.question: Does zero net carbon-dioxide movement prove no respiration?
practice.answer: No. Photosynthesis can be taking up carbon dioxide at the same rate that respiration releases it.
practice.explanation: Subtract opposing rates expressed on the same basis and retain both underlying processes.

commonMistakes: Do not say respiration switches off in daylight.

sections.title: Paper 2B: connect leaf features to gas transfer
paragraphs: A typical leaf is thin, so gases travel short distances between air spaces and cells. Many internal moist cell surfaces provide a large exchange area. Spongy-mesophyll air spaces link the stomatal openings with internal tissues.

Stomatal pores provide routes through the epidermis, and guard cells regulate the openings. Their distribution differs between species, so “every leaf has stomata only underneath” is not a universal rule.
The waxy cuticle helps limit water loss rather than providing the main gas-diffusion pathway. Leaf adaptation is a balance: opening pores improves gas access but also permits water-vapour loss.

example.question: Why do air spaces improve access to photosynthetic cells?
steps: They connect stomata with internal surfaces.
Carbon dioxide can diffuse through the spaces to moist cell surfaces.
Short transfer distances support effective gas exchange.
example.explanation: Link each structural feature to distance, area or access.

practice.question: Is the waxy cuticle the main open passage for gases?
practice.answer: No. The stomatal pores are the main regulated openings in the typical model.
practice.explanation: Link each structural feature to distance, area or access.

commonMistakes: Do not turn a typical stomatal pattern into a universal rule.

sections.title: Paper 2B: stomata balance gas access and water loss
paragraphs: A stoma is a pore between guard cells. When the pore opens, carbon dioxide and oxygen can diffuse between the leaf’s internal air spaces and external air. The guard cells regulate access; they do not actively pump every gas molecule.

Changes in guard-cell water content and turgor alter pore width. Greater turgor in the typical model opens the pore; loss of turgor tends to close it. The curved walls and paired shape help produce that movement.

Open pores allow water vapour to leave as well as gas exchange. Water stress can promote closure and limit carbon-dioxide uptake even in daylight. Light is one influence among several, not a guarantee that all stomata remain open.

example.question: Why can stomatal closure reduce both water loss and photosynthesis?
steps: A smaller pore limits water-vapour transfer.
It also restricts carbon-dioxide access to photosynthetic cells.
The plant faces a trade-off rather than simply switching off one independent process.
example.explanation: Explain opening or closure and then its consequences for both gases and water.

practice.question: Do guard cells pump carbon dioxide into the leaf?
practice.answer: No. They regulate pore width; the gas itself moves mainly by diffusion down its gradient.
practice.explanation: Explain opening or closure and then its consequences for both gases and water.

commonMistakes: Do not confuse pore regulation with active transport of carbon dioxide.

sections.title: Paper 2B: compare light conditions using an indicator
paragraphs: Hydrogencarbonate indicator responds to changes related to carbon dioxide in solution. The usual starting reference is red/orange at the atmospheric-equilibrium condition; higher carbon dioxide shifts it towards yellow, and lower carbon dioxide towards purple. Check the supplied indicator’s reference colours rather than treating a colour as an exact gas concentration.

Use comparable healthy leaves in teacher-prepared tubes with equal small indicator volumes and comparable headspaces. Place leaves above the solution to avoid direct contamination. Compare bright light, dim light and darkness over the same interval, with a no-leaf tube as a background comparison.

Control temperature, leaf species/area, starting indicator condition and exposure time. A lamp can warm the apparatus, and uneven leaf condition can change respiratory as well as photosynthetic rates. A no-leaf comparison for each condition gives stronger evidence if conditions themselves affect the indicator.

Expected purple in suitable bright light supports net carbon-dioxide removal; yellow in darkness supports net addition. Dim light may leave the reference colour when rates balance, but“dim” does not guarantee compensation. No colour outcomes have been measured here.

example.question: A leaf tube stays red/orange under a dim light. What is a supported explanation and one limit?
steps: Photosynthetic carbon-dioxide uptake may approximately balance respiratory release.
The observation concerns net exchange, not an absence of both processes.
Indicator sensitivity and leaf health must be considered before treating it as an exact compensation measurement.
example.explanation: Interpret the carbon-dioxide change with a working reference and controlled conditions.

practice.question: Does hydrogencarbonate indicator directly measure oxygen concentration?
practice.answer: No. It responds to carbon-dioxide-related changes, so oxygen exchange is inferred from additional biological knowledge.
practice.explanation: Interpret the carbon-dioxide change with a working reference and controlled conditions.

commonMistakes: Do not treat an expected colour as an obtained experimental result.

apparatus: Comparable healthy leaves and matched transparent tubes
Light source, foil/dim-light covering, timer and thermometer
method: Record equal starting indicator colour, volume and headspace; keep leaves above the liquid.
Compare bright, dim and dark treatments with a no-leaf background comparison.
Maintain comparable temperature and exposure interval; record actual final colours.
Repeat and compare with the reference chart before inferring net carbon-dioxide changes.
variables: Vary light; observe the carbon-dioxide-related indicator response.
Control temperature, leaf area/species, indicator volume/headspace and exposure time.
safety: Teacher prepares indicator and handles glass/leaf supports; use eye protection as instructed.
Keep lamp heat controlled and electrical equipment away from liquids.
quality: A no-leaf comparison under each condition helps detect direct setup effects.
Colour is not a calibrated gas-exchange rate or oxygen test.

sections.title: Paper 2B: evaluate what the indicator can establish
paragraphs: An indicator records a response to its chemical environment, not a direct count of photosynthetic or respiratory events. A colour shift needs a no-leaf control, stable starting colour and evidence that contamination or temperature effects do not explain the pattern.

Limewater is useful for detecting added carbon dioxide, but is less suitable for distinguishing increases and decreases around an atmospheric starting level. Hydrogencarbonate indicator allows comparison of both directions under the stated conditions.

Use repeats and a reference colour chart or approved colour measurement. Different indicator volumes and headspaces can change response timing. A larger volume does not automatically give a faster change and a single shade is not a calibrated rate.

Leave the gas-exchange and photosynthesis claims proportional to the evidence. A non-changing tube could reflect balanced rates, low sensitivity or an unhealthy leaf, so a working light-treatment comparison matters.

example.question: Why can a no-leaf tube be useful even if it stays at the starting colour?
steps: It supports stability of the indicator and surroundings without the leaf.
A leaf-specific difference is then more plausibly linked to metabolism.
It does not alone rule out all leaf damage or treatment confounds.
example.explanation: State both the supported interpretation and limits of the measurement system.

practice.question: Would adding more indicator necessarily make the response quicker?
practice.answer: No. The gas amount, solution volume, headspace and chemistry affect the response; more indicator is not automatically better.
practice.explanation: State both the supported interpretation and limits of the measurement system.

commonMistakes: No colour change has more than one possible explanation.
